title: India's Naval Chief Visits Mauritius as Defence Outreach to Africa Expands
excerpt: Admiral Krishna Swaminathan's four-day trip and an Indian Army contingent's march in Côte d'Ivoire's Independence Day parade mark New Delhi's growing military footprint across Africa.
body:
• Chief of Naval Staff Admiral Krishna Swaminathan is in Mauritius from August 10–13, 2026, for talks on maritime security, capacity building and military-to-military cooperation.
  • A 60-member Indian Army contingent marched in Côte d'Ivoire's 66th Independence Day parade on August 7, underscoring India's expanding defence diplomacy in West Africa.
  • The twin engagements reflect India's push to deepen its strategic footprint across the Indian Ocean and Africa, where it competes with China and Western powers for influence.

Naval Chief's Mauritius Visit

Admiral Krishna Swaminathan, India's Chief of the Naval Staff, arrived in Mauritius on August 10 for a four-day official visit that will run through August 13, according to the Times of India. During his stay, Admiral Swaminathan is scheduled to meet senior members of the Mauritian government and hold talks on maritime security, defence cooperation, capacity building and military-to-military collaboration.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2086660326314119218

That the newly appointed navy chief chose Mauritius among his earliest overseas engagements is being read as a signal of the importance New Delhi attaches to the island nation. "The visit reinforces what has been described as a robust strategic partnership between India and Mauritius," the Times of India reported.

A Deep Maritime Partnership

The Indian Navy has for years worked closely with the Mauritius National Coast Guard, conducting joint training exercises, carrying out Exclusive Economic Zone surveillance, exchanging port calls and undertaking hydrographic surveys. Mauritius has been a regular participant in major Indian Navy platforms including the Indian Ocean Naval Symposium, MILAN, the International Fleet Review, the Goa Maritime Conclave and Exercise AIKEYME.

These engagements fall under India's MAHASAGAR initiative — Mutual and Holistic Advancement for Security and Growth Across Regions — and the broader SAGAR (Security and Growth for All in the Region) policy, which has trained African maritime and military personnel at Indian institutes and enhanced information-sharing through regional coordination centers, according to Africa Defense Forum.

"India has recognized the varying priorities of African countries and has fine-tuned its own ways of maritime security cooperation in order to effectively respond to the emerging challenges."

— Abhishek Mishra, Manohar Parrikar Institute for Defence Studies and Analyses

India's strategic infrastructure investments in the region have deepened its footprint. In 2023, India built a major airstrip and jetty on Agaléga, a Mauritian island in the southwestern Indian Ocean. The airstrip can handle Boeing P-8I surveillance and anti-submarine warfare aircraft, enabling maritime patrols over the Mozambique Channel and observation of shipping routes around southern Africa, according to Africa Defense Forum.

Indian Army Marches in Côte d'Ivoire

In a parallel development highlighting India's expanding defence engagement in Africa, a 60-member Indian Army contingent drawn from the Regiment of Artillery participated in the military parade marking Côte d'Ivoire's 66th Independence Day on August 7. The contingent, led by Major Sandeep Dhillon, was flown to Abidjan aboard an Indian Air Force IL-76 aircraft at the invitation of the Ivorian government.

The parade was presided over by Ivorian President Alassane Ouattara and attended by India's Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh, along with heads of state from Guinea, Gabon and Benin. India opened a defence wing in Abidjan in January 2025, and in the 18 months since, it has become one of Côte d'Ivoire's leading military training partners, according to the Times of India.

Competing for Influence

The twin engagements come as major powers vie for influence across the Indian Ocean and the African continent. India has stepped up defence exports, joint exercises and training programs with African nations, positioning itself as an alternative to Chinese and Western military partnerships. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar earlier announced the appointment of a Defence Attaché in Mauritius and negotiations on an oil and gas supply agreement, according to Devdiscourse.

In April 2025, India and 10 African countries completed the Africa-India Key Maritime Engagement (Aikeyme), a first-of-its-kind naval exercise co-hosted with Tanzania in Dar es Salaam. Nine African countries — including Mauritius — are members of the Indian Ocean Rim Association, where India assumed the chairmanship in November 2025.

The Diaspora Connection

Mauritius holds a unique position in India's Africa strategy, in part because roughly two-thirds of its 1.3 million population traces ancestry to the Indian subcontinent — the largest Indian-origin community proportionally in any country. Cultural and familial ties have long underpinned the diplomatic relationship, and defence cooperation has built on that foundation. For the broader Indian diaspora across Africa, New Delhi's expanding military presence is also framed as a security umbrella for citizens and communities abroad.

What's Next

Admiral Swaminathan's visit is expected to produce concrete outcomes on operational cooperation between the Indian Navy and the Mauritius National Coast Guard. India continues to expand its network of defence wings across Africa — Abidjan, Rabat and other capitals — and defence exports to the continent are a growing priority. The next India-Africa Defence Dialogue and upcoming IORA engagements will test whether this diplomatic push translates into durable strategic partnerships.
